Front: Discipline sanctions, lightest to heaviest: probation → ___ → public reprimand → suspension → disbarment
Back: Private reprimand

Front: Discipline sanctions, lightest to heaviest: probation → private reprimand → public reprimand → ___ → disbarment
Back: Suspension

Front: In a private reprimand, what gets published?
Back: The misconduct, but not the lawyer's name

Front: How long must a disbarred lawyer wait before applying for reinstatement?
Back: 5 years

Front: Reinstatement after disbarment: what burden of proof?
Back: Clear and convincing evidence

Front: Reinstatement after disbarment: what two things must the lawyer prove?
Back: (1) Rehabilitation and (2) compliance with all conditions

Front: Which requires harm to a client: discipline or malpractice?
Back: Malpractice only — Discipline needs no harm.

Front: Who may always practice law without a license?
Back: Anyone representing themselves

Front: Stated purpose of UPL rules (Rule 5.5 cmt. [2])?
Back: Protect the public from unqualified providers — Class point: not to protect lawyers' business.

Front: General rule on nonlawyers selling legal software?
Back: Generally permitted — Some states have tried to ban it; how far it can go is open.

Front: Florida Bar v. Brumbaugh: what may a nonlawyer form-and-typing service NOT do?
Back: Give individualized legal advice

Front: Which case: nonlawyer typed customers' divorce papers, never claimed to be a lawyer, and nobody was harmed?
Back: Florida Bar v. Brumbaugh

Front: A nonlawyer sells blank divorce forms and types in information customers supply. UPL?
Back: No — Brumbaugh allows forms, procedure booklets, and typing.

Front: A nonlawyer reviews a customer's finances and recommends seeking sole custody. UPL?
Back: Yes — Applying law to one person's situation is individualized legal advice (Brumbaugh).

Front: Rule 5.4(a) prohibits sharing what with a nonlawyer?
Back: Legal fees

Front: Rule 5.4(b): when may a lawyer NOT form a partnership with a nonlawyer?
Back: When any of its activities consist of the practice of law

Front: Rule 5.4(d): a lawyer may not practice in a for-profit firm in which a nonlawyer ___.
Back: Owns an interest

Front: Lawyer and accountant form a 50/50 LLC doing estate and tax planning. Clients consent in writing. Can Lawyer be disciplined?
Back: Yes, under Rule 5.4 — Client consent does not cure fee-sharing or a nonlawyer-owned firm.

Front: Which three jurisdictions let lawyers split fees with nonlawyers?
Back: DC, Utah, and Arizona

Front: Rule 5.3: what must a lawyer do about nonlawyer assistants' conduct?
Back: Make reasonable efforts to ensure it is compatible with the Rules

Front: Rule 5.7: do the Rules apply when a lawyer provides law-related (nonlegal) services?
Back: Yes

Front: How does a lawyer not admitted in a state appear in litigation there?
Back: Motion to appear pro hac vice (temporary admission)

Front: Birbrower: is physical presence in the state required for UPL?
Back: No. Sufficient contact with the state is enough — Presence is a factor, not a requirement.

Front: Birbrower: is preparing a client for arbitration the practice of law?
Back: Yes — The legislature later exempted arbitration.

Front: Birbrower: consequence of the NY firm's UPL in California?
Back: Its fee agreement was unenforceable for the California work

Front: Which case: NY lawyers advised client ESQ in California under a CA-law contract, then sued for fees?
Back: Birbrower, Montalbano, Condon & Frank v. Superior Court

Front: Character & fitness: who bears the burden of proof?
Back: The applicant

Front: Character & fitness: who has the final word on admission?
Back: The state's supreme court

Front: In re Chapman: is disclosing past bad acts enough to gain admission?
Back: No. Disclosure is necessary but not sufficient

Front: Which case: applicant disclosed a suit over his father's upholstery business and was still denied?
Back: In re Application of Chapman

Front: In re Hamm: beyond the crime itself, what sank the application?
Back: Lack of candor and responsibility — Not forthright about the killing; excuses for unpaid child support; plagiarized brief.

Front: Which case: applicant killed someone in a marijuana deal, served his sentence, and was denied admission?
Back: In re Hamm

Front: Rest. § 14: client manifests intent to get legal services + lawyer ___ → relationship.
Back: Manifests consent

Front: Rest. § 14: client manifests intent + lawyer stays silent → relationship when?
Back: When the lawyer knows or should know the client reasonably relies on the lawyer

Front: Rest. § 14: besides client intent, what else creates a lawyer-client relationship?
Back: Appointment by a tribunal

Front: Is a written agreement or a fee required to form a lawyer-client relationship?
Back: No — In re Robbins.

Front: Morris v. Margulis: whose belief decides whether a relationship exists?
Back: The client's subjective belief that he is consulting the lawyer for legal advice

Front: Which case: lawyer recruited his friend as an indemnitor, who thought the lawyer was his lawyer and never got a bill?
Back: In re Robbins

Front: Rule 1.13(a): lawyer retained by a corporation. Who is the client?
Back: The corporation itself, not its officers or employees

Front: Rule 6.2 good cause to decline an appointment: (a) likely rule or law violation, (b) ___, (c) repugnance
Back: Unreasonable financial burden on the lawyer

Front: Rule 6.2 good cause to decline an appointment: (a) ___, (b) unreasonable financial burden, (c) repugnance
Back: Representation likely to violate the Rules or other law

Front: Rule 6.2(c): when does repugnance justify declining an appointment?
Back: When it is likely to impair the relationship or the lawyer's ability to represent

Front: Appointed lawyer objects to the case. Practical next step?
Back: Raise the objection with the court and let it decide

Front: Tennessee Board of Prof. Resp.: is a moral or religious objection alone good cause to decline an appointment?
Back: No

Front: Appointed lawyer believes her criminal client is guilty. Good cause to decline?
Back: No — Tennessee Board: belief in guilt is not a compelling reason.

Front: Nathanson v. MCAD: may a lawyer turn away a client solely because of gender?
Back: No. A law office is a place of public accommodation

Front: Rule 1.16(a) mandatory withdrawal: (1) rule or law violation, (2) ___, (3) client crime or fraud
Back: Lawyer's physical or mental condition materially impairs the representation

Front: Rule 1.16(a) mandatory withdrawal: (1) rule or law violation, (2) lawyer impairment, (3) ___
Back: Client persists in using the lawyer's services for crime or fraud

Front: Rule 1.16(b): may a lawyer permissively withdraw even if it materially harms the client?
Back: Yes

Front: Is a client's nonpayment alone an "unreasonable financial burden"?
Back: No

Front: Rule 1.16(c): court orders the lawyer to keep going, though the lawyer has good cause. Result?
Back: Lawyer must continue — Overrides even a mandatory reason to withdraw.

Front: Rule 1.16(d): lawyer's duty when the representation ends?
Back: Take reasonably practicable steps to protect the client's interests

Front: As trial gets closer, the standard to withdraw gets ___.
Back: Higher

Front: Rule 3.1: what's needed to bring or defend a claim?
Back: A non-frivolous basis in law and fact — A good-faith argument to change the law qualifies.

Front: Whiting v. Lacara: withdrawal on the eve of trial requires what?
Back: Court's consent and good cause

Front: Whiting v. Lacara: why was withdrawal allowed?
Back: Lawyer was stuck between a threatened malpractice suit and making frivolous arguments

Front: Rusinow v. Kamara: can a court deny withdrawal even when the lawyer has good cause?
Back: Yes, when trial is close

Front: Which case: weeks before trial, lawyer learned the client was lying (possible insurance fraud), and withdrawal was denied?
Back: Rusinow v. Kamara

Front: Class problem 2-10: the court orders the lawyer to stay in the case. Answer?
Back: C. He must stay (Rule 1.16(c))

Front: Class problem 2-11: lawyer and client have a material disagreement. Answer?
Back: D. Permissive withdrawal is allowed even with a material adverse effect

Front: Rule 1.1 competence: legal knowledge, skill, ___, and preparation
Back: Thoroughness

Front: Rule 1.1 competence: legal knowledge, ___, thoroughness, and preparation
Back: Skill

Front: Rule 5.1(c)(1): a lawyer is responsible for another lawyer's violation if she ___ it or knowingly ___ it.
Back: Orders it; ratifies it

Front: Rule 5.1(c)(2): when is a supervising lawyer responsible for another lawyer's violation?
Back: She knew in time to prevent or mitigate it but took no reasonable remedial action

Front: Rule 5.3(c): what test makes a lawyer responsible for a nonlawyer's misconduct?
Back: The same two tests as Rule 5.1(c)

Front: Rest. § 48: four elements of professional negligence?
Back: Duty, breach, causation, injury

Front: Rest. § 52: standard of care for lawyers?
Back: Competence and diligence normally exercised by lawyers in similar circumstances

Front: Rest. § 52: does violating an ethics rule by itself create a malpractice claim?
Back: No

Front: When is a lawyer held to a higher standard of care?
Back: When she claims specialized expertise

Front: Rest. § 58(1): is a firm vicariously liable for its lawyers' malpractice?
Back: Yes, except in NY and NJ

Front: Is a firm vicariously liable for its lawyers' discipline?
Back: No. Only for malpractice

Front: Bailey v. Algonquin Gas: client loses because of the lawyer's neglect. Remedy?
Back: Malpractice suit against the lawyer — Client is bound as principal; lawyer is agent.

Front: Which case: lawyer threw away all court mail, and the client lost by default?
Back: Bailey v. Algonquin Gas Transmission Co.

Front: Togstad: can advice to a prospective client create malpractice liability even if the lawyer declines the case?
Back: Yes

Front: Togstad: what should the lawyer have told her?
Back: To see another lawyer (the statute of limitations was running)

Front: Which case: "I don't think you have a case," and the statute of limitations ran?
Back: Togstad v. Vesely, Otto, Miller & Keefe

Front: Rule 1.2(c): two requirements to limit the scope of representation?
Back: Limit is reasonable + client gives informed consent

Front: Rule 1.8(h)(1): when may a lawyer prospectively limit malpractice liability?
Back: Only if the client is independently represented in making the agreement

Front: Rule 1.8(h)(2): settling a malpractice claim with an unrepresented client requires what?
Back: Advising the client in writing to seek independent counsel

Front: Engagement letter caps the lawyer's malpractice liability at $10,000. Client signs without her own lawyer. Valid?
Back: No (Rule 1.8(h)(1)) — A prospective limit needs independent counsel, not just advice to get one.

Front: Are arbitration clauses for malpractice claims allowed?
Back: Yes

Front: Lerner v. Laufer: may a lawyer exclude services normally expected?
Back: Yes, with a clear, signed limitation and informed consent

Front: Which case: divorce lawyer's letter said he would not advise on the settlement because he hadn't reviewed her finances?
Back: Lerner v. Laufer

Front: Strickland prong 1?
Back: Counsel's performance fell below that of a reasonably competent lawyer

Front: Strickland prong 2?
Back: Prejudice: a reasonable probability the result would have been different — The hard prong to meet.

Front: Ineffective assistance of counsel applies in what kind of case?
Back: Criminal only (Sixth Amendment)

Front: Criminal malpractice: what must the client show beyond Strickland's "reasonable probability"?
Back: But for the lawyer's failure, the result would have differed

Front: Rule 1.2(a): who decides the objectives of the representation?
Back: The client

Front: Rule 1.2(a): who decides the means?
Back: The lawyer, after consulting the client

Front: Rule 1.2(a): in a civil case, which decision always belongs to the client?
Back: Whether to settle

Front: Rule 1.2(a) criminal decisions for the client: the plea, ___, and whether to testify
Back: Whether to waive a jury trial

Front: Rule 1.2(a) criminal decisions for the client: the plea, waiving a jury, and ___
Back: Whether the client will testify

Front: Florida Bar v. Stopa: lawyer accepts a settlement without the client's consent. Result?
Back: Violates Rule 1.2(a); disbarred

Front: Rule 1.2 cmt. [2]: fundamental disagreement over means. Options?
Back: Lawyer may withdraw, or client may fire the lawyer

Front: Rule 1.2 cmt. [3]: client gave advance authorization. May the lawyer rely on it?
Back: Yes, absent a material change in circumstances

Front: Client says "Don't bring me offers below $50,000." A $40,000 offer comes in. Must the lawyer relay it?
Back: Not required, but should

Front: Rest. § 21 cmt. d: must a lawyer follow an instruction she reasonably believes is unethical?
Back: No

Front: Rest. § 23 cmt. c: when may a lawyer decide for the client?
Back: When there is no time to consult

Front: Jones v. Barnes: must appointed appellate counsel raise every nonfrivolous issue the client wants?
Back: No. Issue selection is professional judgment

Front: Jones v. Barnes dissent (Brennan, Marshall): who should control issue selection, and why?
Back: The client, because the Sixth Amendment makes counsel an assistant

Front: Boyd v. Brett-Major: is following a client's explicit, informed instruction malpractice?
Back: No, unless the instruction requires crime or fraud

Front: Which case: clients told of an absolute foreclosure defense chose not to raise it to protect a bonding relationship?
Back: Boyd v. Brett-Major

Front: McCoy v. Louisiana: may counsel concede guilt over the defendant's express objection?
Back: No

Front: Florida v. Nixon (vs. McCoy): when may counsel concede guilt?
Back: When the defendant, after consultation, stays silent

Front: Rule 1.2(d): may a lawyer discuss the legal consequences of a client's proposed crime?
Back: Yes. Only counseling or assisting known crime or fraud is barred

Front: Client asks whether a tax plan is legal. Lawyer thinks it's a gray area. May she help him figure out what the law allows?
Back: Yes (Rule 1.2(d)) — A good-faith effort to determine the law's validity, scope, or meaning is allowed.

Front: Rule 8.4(b) misconduct?
Back: Committing a criminal act, including aiding a client's crime

Front: Rule 8.4(c) misconduct?
Back: Conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation

Front: Rule 2.1: besides law, what may a lawyer's advice refer to?
Back: Moral, economic, social, and political factors

Front: Which case: lawyer told a custody client about a safehouse network and helped liquidate her assets?
Back: People v. Chappell

Front: People v. Chappell: which three rules, and what sanction?
Back: 1.2(d), 8.4(b), 8.4(c); disbarred

Front: Rule 1.14(a): client has diminished capacity. Lawyer's baseline duty?
Back: Maintain a normal relationship as far as reasonably possible

Front: Rule 1.14(b): is protective action (e.g., seeking a guardian) required or permitted?
Back: Permitted, not required

Front: Rule 1.14(b): protective action requires diminished capacity + inability to act in own interest + ___
Back: Risk of substantial physical, financial, or other harm

Front: Gilmore v. Utah: may a competent defendant waive appeal of a death sentence?
Back: Yes, if the waiver is knowing and intelligent

Front: Gilmore v. Utah: why did his mother's "next friend" petition fail?
Back: He was competent and had his own counsel

Front: Class problem 2-21. Answer and principle?
Back: B. Objectives vs. means

Front: Rule 7.3(a) solicitation: targeted to a specific person + known need in a particular matter + ___
Back: Offer to provide legal services for that matter

Front: Does "live person-to-person contact" include texts or chat rooms?
Back: No — Live = in person, live phone, real-time video or audio.

Front: Rule 7.3(b): live solicitation is banned when a significant motive is ___.
Back: Pecuniary gain

Front: Rule 7.3(b) exceptions: (1) another lawyer, (2) ___, (3) routine business user
Back: Family, close personal, or prior business or professional relationship

Front: Rule 7.3(b) exceptions: (1) ___, (2) family or prior relationship, (3) routine business user
Back: Another lawyer

Front: Rule 7.3(b) exceptions: (1) another lawyer, (2) family or prior relationship, (3) ___
Back: Someone who routinely uses that type of legal service for business

Front: Rule 7.3(c): even within an exception, when is solicitation barred?
Back: Target said they don't want it, or it involves coercion, duress, or harassment

Front: Lawyer calls a stranger she read was in a car crash and offers to take the case. Allowed?
Back: No — Live phone + pecuniary motive + no exception.

Front: Lawyer texts a car-crash victim offering representation. Barred by Rule 7.3(b)?
Back: No. Texts aren't live contact — Still subject to Rule 7.1 (no misleading statements).

Front: Lawyer phones a former client about a new matter he needs help with. Allowed?
Back: Yes — Prior professional relationship exception.

Front: Lawyer visits a hospital to sign up an accident victim; she says she isn't interested. Lawyer comes back the next day. Allowed?
Back: No — Rule 7.3(b) and (c).

Front: Rule 7.3(e): may a prepaid legal plan use live contact to enroll members?
Back: Yes, if targets aren't known to need help in a particular matter

Front: Ohralik: does a ban on in-person solicitation for pecuniary gain violate the First Amendment?
Back: No

Front: Which case: lawyer signed an accident victim in the hospital to a one-third contingency and secretly recorded her parents?
Back: Ohralik v. Ohio State Bar Ass'n

Front: In re Primus: may a state punish a nonprofit lawyer's solicitation for political or ideological goals?
Back: No. The rule must survive exacting scrutiny

Front: Which case: ACLU lawyer offered free representation to women sterilized as a Medicaid condition?
Back: In re Primus

Front: Ohralik vs. Primus: the key fact that changes the outcome?
Back: Pecuniary gain (Ohralik) vs. nonprofit ideological expression (Primus)

Front: Which case: lawyer paid a minister to pray with hospital patients' families and hand out his card?
Back: Florida Bar v. Barrett

Front: Usual sanction for paying a third party to solicit clients?
Back: Severe discipline, usually disbarment

Front: Which Supreme Court case first allowed lawyer advertising?
Back: Bates

Front: Rule 7.1: two ways a communication is misleading?
Back: A material misstatement of fact or law, or a misleading omission

Front: A truthful ad about past results is misleading when?
Back: When a reasonable person would expect the same result — A disclaimer can cure it.

Front: Rule 7.2(c): two requirements to claim you're a certified specialist?
Back: Certified by an approved or ABA-accredited body + that body is clearly named

Front: Rule 7.2(d): what must every lawyer advertisement include?
Back: Name and contact info of at least one responsible lawyer or firm

Front: Lawyer pays a TV station for an ad. Paying for a recommendation?
Back: No. Reasonable costs of permitted ads are allowed (Rule 7.2(b)(1))

Front: Lawyer pays a friend $200 for each client she refers. Allowed?
Back: No (Rule 7.2(b))

Front: Lawyer sends a referring lawyer a $25 gift card as thanks, not promised in advance. Allowed?
Back: Yes. Nominal gift of appreciation (Rule 7.2(b)(5))

Front: Two lawyers agree to refer to each other; clients are told; the deal is non-exclusive. Allowed?
Back: Yes. Reciprocal referral agreement (Rule 7.2(b)(4))

Front: May a firm use a trade name?
Back: Yes, unless it implies a government, public, or charitable legal services connection

Front: May a firm keep the name of a partner now holding public office?
Back: Not while that lawyer isn't actively practicing with the firm

Front: Matter of Zang: is misleading lawyer advertising protected commercial speech?
Back: No, and no actual harm is needed

Front: Which case: ads portrayed inexperienced lawyers as seasoned trial lawyers?
Back: Matter of Zang

Front: Rule 1.5(a): what kind of fee or expense is prohibited?
Back: An unreasonable one

Front: Rule 1.5(b): what must be communicated to the client about fees?
Back: Scope of the representation and the basis or rate of the fee and expenses

Front: Rule 1.5(b): must the fee basis be in writing?
Back: Preferably, but not required (contingent fees are the exception)

Front: ABA Op. 93-379: may a lawyer bill clients for overhead?
Back: No

Front: ABA Op. 93-379: how much may a lawyer charge for third-party disbursements?
Back: Actual cost, unless she incurs added costs

Front: Lawyer spends 4 hours on work that benefits 3 clients equally. How many hours may she bill in total?
Back: 4 — Not 12: no double billing.

Front: Matter of Ledingham: when is a fee unreasonable?
Back: When it is grossly out of proportion to the work required

Front: Which case: $120,000 fee on a routine ~30-hour matter, including time spent learning Vermont law?
Back: Matter of Ledingham

Front: Which case: lawyer billed each of 41 malpractice cases for the entire time he was at court?
Back: In re Berg (double billing)

Front: Cincinnati Bar v. Alsfelder: may a lawyer bill for non-legal life advice if the client was told?
Back: No

Front: Which case: $30,000 billed for weekly calls about a client's driveway complaints?
Back: Cincinnati Bar Ass'n v. Alsfelder

Front: Which case: lawyer billed divorce clients for time filling out her time sheets and was disbarred?
Back: Attorney Grievance Comm'n v. Kreamer

Front: Rule 1.5(c): who must sign a contingent fee agreement?
Back: The client

Front: Rule 1.5(c): the agreement must say whether expenses are deducted ___ or ___ the fee is calculated.
Back: Before or after

Front: Rule 1.5(c): what must the lawyer give the client at the end of a contingent fee matter?
Back: A written statement of the outcome and the remittance

Front: Rule 1.5(d): two matters where contingent fees are banned?
Back: Divorce, alimony, support, or property settlement; criminal defense

Front: Lawyer agrees to represent a criminal defendant for 20% of anything saved on fines. Allowed?
Back: No (Rule 1.5(d)(2))

Front: Lawyer's fee in a divorce is 10% of the alimony award. Allowed?
Back: No (Rule 1.5(d)(1))

Front: Contingent fee justification: (1) ___, (2) incentive to win and screen weak claims, (3) risk-sharing
Back: Access for clients who can't otherwise afford a lawyer

Front: Contingent fee justification: (1) access, (2) ___, (3) risk-sharing
Back: Incentive to win and screen out weak claims

Front: Contingent fee justification: (1) access, (2) incentive and screening, (3) ___
Back: Client shares risk with a lawyer better able to bear it

Front: Can a contingent fee still be unreasonable?
Back: Yes, if little or no work is involved

Front: Mid-litigation, lawyer asks the client to raise her contingency from 33% to 40%. How will a court view it?
Back: With special scrutiny; generally not allowed (Rest. § 18 cmt. e)

Front: Client voids the fee contract. What does the lawyer get?
Back: Fair value of the services (Rest. § 39)

Front: Rule 1.5(e) fee split between firms: (1) ___, (2) client agrees in writing to each share, (3) total is reasonable
Back: Split is proportional to work, or each lawyer assumes joint responsibility

Front: Rule 1.5(e) fee split between firms: (1) proportional or joint responsibility, (2) ___, (3) total is reasonable
Back: Client agrees, including each lawyer's share, confirmed in writing

Front: Rule 1.8(a) business deal with client: (1) fair terms disclosed in writing, (2) ___, (3) signed informed consent
Back: Written advice to seek independent counsel, with time to do so

Front: Rule 1.8(a) business deal with client: (1) ___, (2) advice to get independent counsel, (3) signed informed consent
Back: Fair and reasonable terms, fully disclosed in writing

Front: May a lawyer accept property as a fee?
Back: Yes, but it may be a business transaction under Rule 1.8(a)

Front: Rule 1.8(d): when may a lawyer get media rights to the client's story?
Back: Only after the representation ends

Front: Rule 1.8(f): third party pays the fee. Three conditions?
Back: Client's informed consent, no interference with the lawyer's judgment, confidentiality protected

Front: Rule 1.8(e): may a lawyer advance court costs repayable only if the client wins?
Back: Yes

Front: During a suit, lawyer covers a poor client's rent as a modest gift, not promised or advertised. Allowed?
Back: Yes. Modest pro bono gift for living expenses (Rule 1.8(e)(3))

Front: Lawyer advertises "We'll pay your bills while your case is pending." Allowed?
Back: No (Rule 1.8(e)) — Living-expense gifts can't be promised in advance or advertised.

Front: Rule 1.8(i): two exceptions to the ban on owning part of the lawsuit?
Back: A lien authorized by law; a reasonable contingent fee in a civil case

Front: In a patent case, lawyer takes a 10% ownership interest in the patent as her fee. Allowed?
Back: No. Proprietary interest in the subject of litigation (Rule 1.8(i))

Front: Rule 1.15: how long must trust account records be kept?
Back: 5 years

Front: Rule 1.15(b): when may a lawyer put her own money in the trust account?
Back: Only to pay bank service charges

Front: Rule 1.15(c): advance fees go where, and until when?
Back: Into the trust account, until earned

Front: Rule 1.15(e): what happens to the disputed part of client funds?
Back: It stays separate until the dispute is resolved — Undisputed portions are distributed promptly.

Front: Court-awarded fees: what method do courts use?
Back: The lodestar, presumed sufficient

Front: Statutory fee awards belong to whom?
Back: The client

Front: Perdue v. Kenny A.: is a great result enough to enhance the lodestar?
Back: No. Only extraordinary circumstances the lodestar doesn't already reflect

Front: Attorney-client privilege is what kind of rule?
Back: A rule of evidence

Front: Work product protection is what kind of rule?
Back: A rule of discovery

Front: The duty of confidentiality is what kind of rule?
Back: An ethical rule

Front: Does privilege protect the underlying facts?
Back: No. Only the communications

Front: Work product protects materials prepared in anticipation of ___.
Back: Litigation

Front: Work product: when can a judge order disclosure?
Back: Substantial need + undue hardship

Front: Confidentiality vs. privilege: which covers information from third parties?
Back: Confidentiality (all information relating to the representation, any source)

Front: Rule 1.6(a): three ways a lawyer may reveal client information?
Back: Informed consent, implied authorization, or a 1.6(b) exception

Front: Are the Rule 1.6(b) exceptions mandatory or permissive?
Back: Permissive ("may reveal")

Front: Client tells his lawyer he plans to kill a witness tomorrow. May the lawyer reveal it?
Back: Yes (Rule 1.6(b)(1)) — Reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm.

Front: Client is using the lawyer's drafting to run an investor fraud. May the lawyer reveal it to stop it?
Back: Yes (Rule 1.6(b)(2)) — Requires substantial financial injury and use of the lawyer's services.

Front: The client's fraud (done using the lawyer's services) is already finished. May the lawyer reveal to mitigate the loss?
Back: Yes (Rule 1.6(b)(3))

Front: Client sues the lawyer for malpractice. May the lawyer use client information in defense?
Back: Yes (Rule 1.6(b)(5))

Front: Lawyer calls an ethics expert for advice on her own duties. May she share client information?
Back: Yes (Rule 1.6(b)(4))

Front: A court orders the lawyer to produce client information. May she comply?
Back: Yes (Rule 1.6(b)(6))

Front: Lawyer moving firms shares limited client information to run a conflicts check. Allowed?
Back: Yes, if privilege isn't compromised (Rule 1.6(b)(7))

Front: Rule 1.6(c): lawyer's duty to safeguard client information?
Back: Reasonable efforts to prevent inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure or access

Front: Privilege elements: communication (1) between client and counsel, (2) ___, (3) for legal advice
Back: Intended to be and actually kept confidential

Front: Privilege elements: communication (1) between client and counsel, (2) kept confidential, (3) ___
Back: Made to obtain or provide legal advice

Front: Client hires a lawyer for work a nonlawyer could do just as well. Privileged?
Back: No. Ask whether the work is primarily legal

Front: Kovel: does privilege cover nonlawyers helping the lawyer give legal advice?
Back: Yes (accountants, assistants, summer associates)

Front: Client shares IPO details with the lawyer that will appear in the prospectus. Privileged?
Back: No. Information meant to go public isn't confidential — Discussion of whether to disclose it is privileged.

Front: Rest. § 72: client consults someone she reasonably believes is a lawyer, but isn't. Privileged?
Back: Yes

Front: Rest. § 70: who are "privileged persons"?
Back: Client (incl. prospective), lawyer, and agents who facilitate the communication or representation

Front: Rest. § 71: when is a communication "in confidence"?
Back: When the speaker reasonably believes only privileged persons will learn it

Front: FRE 501: which privilege law applies in federal court?
Back: Federal common law, except state law for civil claims governed by state law

Front: In re County of Erie: test for mixed legal and policy advice?
Back: Predominant purpose is legal advice → privileged

Front: Which case: county lawyer's emails on strip-search policy were held privileged?
Back: In re County of Erie

Front: Upjohn: whose communications with company lawyers can be privileged?
Back: Employees at any level, if made to secure legal advice for the company

Front: Which case: internal investigation of foreign bribes; IRS sought employee questionnaires?
Back: Upjohn Co. v. United States

Front: People v. Meredith: defense moves physical evidence. Is its original location privileged?
Back: No

Front: Which case: defense investigator dug up the wallet the client had buried?
Back: People v. Meredith ("Scott" in your notes)

Front: Client tells his lawyer where he hid the gun. Lawyer goes and looks but leaves it there. Is what she saw privileged?
Back: Yes — Observations from a privileged communication are covered unless the defense moves or alters the evidence.
